summary: The note explains the ancient Egyptian division into Upper and Lower Egypt and how their unification around c. 3000 BC was reflected in royal regalia. Each region had its own crown, and the pharaohs' combined double crown symbolized rule over both. It also notes the tradition that Menes, identified with Narmer, was the unifying king, as shown on the Narmer Palette.
one_line: Describes how the kingdoms of Upper and Lower Egypt were united around 3000 BC and symbolized through their distinct royal crowns.
key_facts: The kingdoms of Upper and Lower Egypt were united c. 3000 BC.
Each kingdom maintained its own regalia after the unification.
Upper Egypt's regalia was the hedjet, also called the White Crown.
Lower Egypt's regalia was the deshret, also called the Red Crown.
Pharaohs were known as the rulers of the Two Lands.
The pschent was a double crown in which each half represented sovereignty of one of the kingdoms.
Ancient Egyptian tradition credited Menes as the king who united Upper and Lower Egypt.
Menes is now believed to be the same person as Narmer.
On the Narmer Palette the king is depicted wearing the Red Crown in one scene.
On the Narmer Palette the king is depicted wearing the White Crown in another scene.
The Narmer Palette's depiction shows the king's rule over both Lands.
